Let's see what happens when Wally discovers something unexpected and learns how important water is for all his friends. So, snuggle in, get comfy, and let's begin Wally's story together. Deep in the warm Australian bush, there lived a cheerful little wombat named Wally. Wally had one favorite thing in the whole world. Digging. He dug in the soft sand, under the shady gums, and sometimes even under the rocks near the creek. Scratch, scratch, scratch went his strong claws as he dug. Wally loved making tunnels. They kept him cool on hot days and cozy at night. One bright morning, Wally started digging a brand new burrow. He dug deeper and deeper, humming a little tune to himself. And then suddenly, clunk, his claws hit something hard and shiny. "Ah! What's this?" Wally wondered. He scratched again. Clunk, clunk, and then whoosh! A great stream of water sprayed high into the air. It sparkled like a fountain, glistening in the sunlight. Wally gasped in surprise. And then his eyes lit up. "Wowee! A fountain just for me!" he laughed. He twirled in the spray, rolled in the puddles, and splashed his paws. The cool water rained down on his fur, and Wally giggled with delight. This is the best playground ever. But while Wally played down at the creek, Freddy the frog was having a very different day. Freddy sat on his favorite lily pad, blinking nervously as the water around him sank lower and lower. "Ribbit, what's happening?" Freddy croked. "My pond is shrinking. My lily pad is wobbling. Oh no. Oh no. Just then, Max the Magpie swooped down from a tall gum tree. He flapped his wings and called out, "Freddy, what's wrong?" "My water is disappearing!" Freddy cried. Soon my pond will be gone forever. Max tilted his head and listened. In the distance, he heard a strange spraying sound. He followed it and soon found Wally still spinning in the fountain of water. Wally. Max squalked. What have you done? Wally stopped midsplash, dripping wet. Hello, Max. Isn't this amazing? Look at my fountain. But Max frowned. This is not a fountain. That's a water pipe. You've broken it while digging. That water is supposed to flow to the creek. Freddy's pond is drying up because of this. Wally's smile faded. He looked around at the muddy mess and then back at Max. Oh no, I didn't know. I just thought it was fun. His ears drooped sadly. Freddy hopped up behind Max. Without water, I can't live in my pond. Please, can you fix it? Wally felt awful. He never wanted to hurt his friends. But how do I fix a pipe? He asked softly. Max ruffled his feathers. I've seen humans fix things like this before. They use something sticky and shiny tape. If I can find some, maybe we can patch it. With that, Max soared high into the sky. He flapped across the bush until he spotted a quiet campsite. On the edge of the camp sat a roll of silver tape. Quick as a flash, Max picked it up in his beak and flew back to Wally and Freddy. "Got it!" he chirped proudly. "Brilliant," Freddy croked. Wally carefully took the roll in his paws. He rolled out the sticky tape and began to press a strip over the crack in the pipe. Wally pressed the tape firmly with his strong paws. Freddy pointed. A little more over to the left, Wally. Slowly, the spray grew smaller and smaller until at last the water stopped. Only a gentle drip remained. The friends cheered together. Hooray! We did it! And the water began to flow back towards the creek. Freddy hopped happily as his pond filled once more. He splashed onto his lily pad and croked with relief. Home sweet home. Wally sighed, wiping mud from his fur. I guess water isn't just for splashing. It's precious. Without it, the bush and all of us would be in trouble. Max nodded wisely. Exactly, Wally. Water keeps our world alive. Every drop counts. That evening, the moon shone bright. Wally began to walk back to his burrow, looking at the pond shining under the moonlight. As he curled up in his cozy tunnel, Wally whispered to himself, "I'll always love digging, but next time I'll make sure to dig carefully." And with the gentle sound of the water trickling back into the creek, Wally drifted off to sleep, dreaming of happy ponds, splashing frogs, and the sparkling bush around him. The end. And that was a story of Wally the wombat and the burst pipe, who learned a very special lesson. Water isn't just for splashing and playing. It's precious. and we all need to take care of it. Remember, every drop counts and we all have a part to play in protecting our world. Thank you so much for joining us today. On the golden sands of a quiet Australian beach, the waves whispered as they rolled in and out. Tiny crabs scured sideways, leaving trails behind them, and seagulls flew high in the sky. Among the dunes, a small turtle named Toby poked his head out of the sand. He was only little with his shells still shiny and green. And today was his first big journey making his way from the sand to the sea. Toby blinked at the sparkling water. It doesn't look too far, he thought. If I hurry, I'll get there faster. Excited, he scrambled forward quickly. But his little flippers sank deep into the sand. And before he knew it, plop. Toby tumbled sideways. Toby managed to wobble back onto his belly. Sand sticking to his shell. Toby wanted to get to the water even faster now. Nearby, an older turtle named Aunt Tilda watched kindly. Slow down, Toby, she called. The beach is tricky. Rushing will only make you trip harder. But Toby shook his head. I don't want to be the last one. I want to reach the sea first. So off he went faster this time. His flippers pumped, his shell rocked, and whoosh! He tripped over a little mound of sand, rolling onto his back like an upside down bowl. The crabs giggled, clicking their claws. The water did not hurry, but still came in closer, rolling forward in its own time. He sighed. "So, if I go slowly, I'll still get there." Aunt Tilda nodded. "Slow and steady, little one. Patience is the secret." Toby took a deep breath. This time, instead of rushing, he placed one flipper carefully, then the other. Step by step, he made his way forward. The sand didn't trip him as much. The wind cooled his shell, and he began to notice things he hadn't seen before. Toby wanted to join them, but then he remembered the seagulls laughing, the crabs giggling, and his tumbles. Toby smiled softly and kept moving at his own pace. One by one, the hasty turtles tripped and rolled in the sand. They puffed and panted while Toby kept plotting on, slow, steady, and without falling. At last, after what felt like a long, careful walk, Toby reached the edge of the sea. The cool water lapped at his flippers. It sparkled like a thousand stars. Aunt Tilda appeared beside him, her shell glowing in the light of the sunset. You see, Toby, patience carried you safely to the ocean. The sea will always be here waiting for you. Toby's eyes shone. Rushing only made him stumble, but patience carried him exactly where he needed to be. And from that day on, whenever Toby felt the urge to hurry, he remembered the steady rhythm of the waves and smiled. The end. It is perfect for classrooms, families, or just for fun. So, let's find out some amazing, funny, and surprising facts about these furry little tree huggers. Here we go. Fact one. People often call them koala bears, but guess what? They're not bears at all. They're marsupials, just like kangaroos and wombats. Fact two, baby koalas are called joeies. That's the same name given to all massupial babies, whether it's a kangaroo, wombat, or koala. Fact three, koala moms can carry their tiny babies in a tummy pouch for about 6 months, snuggly and safe. Fact four. Koalas are nap champions. Koalas are the world's sleepiest animals, snoozing up to 18 to 20 hours every day. Fact five. Koalas eat almost nothing but eucalyptus leaves. Not yummy for us, but perfect for them. Fact six, koalas have a builtin eucalyptus filter. Eucalyptus leaves can be poisonous, but koalas have a special digestive system that removes toxins. Super clever. Fact seven. Koalas are amazing tree climbers. They even have two thumbs on each front paw, which helps them grip branches tightly. Fact eight, koalas have fingerprints just like humans. If you look closely at a koala's paw, you'd see fingerprints that look almost exactly like ours. Scientists sometimes have trouble telling them apart. Fact nine. Koalas hug trees not just to rest, but to also cool down on hot Aussy days. Fact 10. The word koala comes from an Aboriginal word meaning no water because they get most of their water from eucalyptus leaves. Fact 11. Even though they look quiet, koalas can make very loud grunts and bellows, a bit like snores and roars. [Music] Fact 12. Furry bottoms. Koalas have thick padded bottoms almost like cushions so they can sit comfortably in trees for hours. Fact 13. Koalas are excellent jumpers. Koalas can leap from one branch to another with surprising strength even though they look slow and sleepy. Fact 14. Koalas are nocturnal, which means they are most active at night. That's when they munch on eucalyptus leaves under the moonlight. Fact 15. Koalas are extremely slow eaters. Eating takes a long time because koalas chew their leaves very slowly and carefully. Fact 16. Koalas have big, sensitive noses that help them find the freshest and tastiest eucalyptus leaves. Fact 17. Just like people, koalas from different places in Australia make slightly different sounds, almost like having an accent. Fact 18. Koalas are super clingy babies. After leaving the pouch, joies cling tightly to their mom's belly or back for another 6 months. Fact 19. Koalas live high in eucalyptus trees. They rarely come down to the ground unless they need to move to another tree. Fact 20. Koalas are native only to Australia. Koalas are found nowhere else in the world except in Australia's eucalyptus forests. That makes them a true Aussie icon. And that's it. 20 fun facts about koalas. From their big sleepy naps to their special treehugging habits, koalas are some of the most unique animals in the world. Which fact was your favorite?
